basic_information.official_title: AN ACT APPROPRIATING SUPPLEMENTAL FUNDS FOR THE OPERATION OF THE BANGSAMORO GOVERNMENT AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
basic_information.effectivity: 15 days after publication in any newspaper of general circulation in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: An ₱8.44 billion top-up to the 2024 regional budget — funded not by new money but out of appropriations from earlier years that were never spent.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: Unutilised prior-year appropriations had accumulated in the Bangsamoro Treasury. Rather than let them lapse, Parliament re-appropriated them across 17 ministries, offices and commissions.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: ₱8.44 billion is released, with agriculture taking 43.6% of it and public works, health and the interior ministry taking most of the rest. The money is available for obligation until 31 December 2025, after which unreleased appropriations lapse and unobligated funds revert to the Treasury.
who_will_be_affected: Farmers and fisherfolk, through the ₱3.68 billion agriculture allocation
Communities awaiting roads, water supply and flood control
Patients and health workers, through ₱1 billion for health programmes
Barangay health workers, with ₱124.6 million of their own
Learners, through ₱375.8 million for education including school buildings
Disaster-affected communities, through ₱512.3 million for rapid emergency response
citizen_summary.when_will_it_take_effect: In force since 2024 — approved by the Chief Minister on 14 October 2024, effective 15 days after publication. The appropriations were valid for obligation until 31 December 2025.

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: NOW LAW, and now expired for new obligations. This was ₱8.44 billion of previously unspent money put back to work in 2024–2025. If a road, health programme or farm input reached your community in that window, this act may be where it came from.
in_practice: ₱8,441,261,975 total, across 17 ministries, offices and commissions
The money came from unutilised prior years' appropriations held in the Bangsamoro Treasury, not from new revenue
Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform received ₱3.68 billion — 43.6% of the whole act
Public Works received ₱1.21 billion, all capital outlay
Health received ₱1.00 billion, including ₱124.6 million for barangay health workers
Interior and Local Government received ₱956.5 million, of which ₱512.3 million for rapid emergency action on disasters
Funds were available for obligation only until 31 December 2025
Unreleased appropriations lapse; unobligated funds revert to the Treasury for reappropriation

for_specific_groups.Farmers, fisherfolk and agrarian reform: ₱3.68 billion — ₱2.98 billion for the Basic Integration for Harmonized Intervention programme, ₱633.9 million for aquaculture and capture fisheries, and ₱60.5 million for land acquisition for poor agrarian reform beneficiaries.
for_specific_groups.Patients and health workers: ₱1.00 billion, including ₱298.4 million for non-communicable disease, ₱237.4 million for the Tiyakap Bangsamoro Kalusugan programme, ₱124.6 million for barangay health workers, ₱121.1 million for nutrition, and ₱65.6 million for surgical outreach.
for_specific_groups.Communities awaiting infrastructure: ₱1.21 billion in public works capital outlay — ₱704.5 million for other infrastructure, ₱294.6 million for road network development, ₱141.0 million for water supply and ₱25.2 million for flood management.
for_specific_groups.Learners and schools: ₱375.8 million for education — ₱174.0 million for school-based management and operations, ₱142.3 million for management support, ₱29.9 million for technical-vocational provisions, ₱14.0 million for school sports and ₱9.6 million for madaris education services.
for_specific_groups.Workers: ₱148.4 million for employment facilitation and promotion, including ₱104.1 million in financial assistance and subsidy and ₱27.5 million in labour and wages.
for_specific_groups.Young people: ₱69.5 million for the Bangsamoro Youth Commission, almost all of it training and scholarship expenses.
for_specific_groups.Indigenous peoples: ₱3.4 million for the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs — 0.04% of the act, and the smallest agency allocation in it.
for_specific_groups.Communities in conflict: ₱271.7 million for public order and safety, including ₱168.5 million for peacebuilding initiatives and ₱39.0 million for alternative dispute resolution.

what_this_means_for_you.where_this_applies: The whole BARMM, with funds released directly to ministries, offices and agencies including their provincial offices.
what_this_means_for_you.when_you_will_feel_it: The obligation window closed on 31 December 2025; delivery, inspection and payment continued until funds were fully expended.
what_you_can_do: Check ministry websites for infrastructure project disclosures — Section 13 requires the project title, location, description, budget estimates and winning contractor to be posted within 30 days of contract signing, and the actual cost and any variation orders within 30 days of completion
Look for the agency's status report on Commission on Audit findings, due within 60 days of the annual audit report and required to be posted on the agency website
If reports are missing, note that Section 12 automatically suspends the salaries of the responsible officials until they comply
watch_out_for: This act spends money that earlier budgets failed to spend. ₱8.44 billion of accumulated underspending is itself a finding about the region's absorptive capacity.
Agriculture took 43.6% of the act in a single allocation.
The Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs received ₱3.4 million — less than a tenth of what the Darul-Ifta' received.
Engineering and administrative overhead of up to 1%, plus administrative costs of up to 3%, may be deducted from projects costing more than ₱1,000,000.
This registry has read the full act, but it records agency and programme totals rather than every object-of-expenditure line.

key_terms_explained.Supplemental appropriation: A budget law passed during the year to add to what the annual appropriations act already provided.
key_terms_explained.Unutilised prior years' appropriations: Money appropriated in earlier budgets that was never obligated or released, sitting in the Treasury. This act's entire funding source.
key_terms_explained.SARO: Special Allotment Release Order — the document authorising an agency to actually commit money against an appropriation.
key_terms_explained.MOOE: Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses — day-to-day running costs, as distinct from salaries and capital outlay.
key_terms_explained.Capital outlay: Spending on assets that last — buildings, roads, equipment, vehicles.
key_terms_explained.Cash budgeting system: Appropriations valid for obligation only within a fixed window, after which they lapse.
key_terms_explained.Certification of Availability of Funds: The chief accountant's certificate that money exists for a contract, required before any obligation is incurred.
key_terms_explained.EAO: Engineering and Administrative Overhead — a percentage deducted from infrastructure project funds for supervision costs.

for_citizens: None. An appropriations act imposes no duty on the public.
for_agencies: Secure a Special Allotment Release Order before obligating appropriations
Obtain a Certification of Availability of Funds from the chief accountant, made part of every contract, before incurring any obligation
Obtain the Chief Minister's Authority to Purchase Motor Vehicle before procuring any transportation equipment
Adhere strictly to government procurement laws
Submit monthly, quarterly or yearly financial and physical accountability reports through the Unified Reporting System, in hardcopy to the finance ministry, and on the agency website

what_is_prohibited: Incurring an obligation without first securing a Certification of Availability of Funds from the agency's chief accountant.
Procuring transportation equipment without the Chief Minister's Authority to Purchase Motor Vehicle.

Treating funds transferred between organisational units, between agencies, or to LGUs as disbursed before the goods, works or services have actually been delivered, inspected and accepted within the validity period.
Deducting engineering and administrative overhead above 1%, or administrative costs above 3%, of project costs for projects over ₱1,000,000.
Obligating appropriations after the validity period.

penalties.for_citizens: None. The act creates no offence.
penalties.for_officials: Failure to submit the required financial and physical accountability reports results in the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until they comply. Repeated failure or refusal without justifiable cause may be a ground for administrative disciplinary action under civil service rules, with the Minister or Head of Office responsible for enforcing this.

everyday_scenarios: A farmers' association receives seed and equipment support in 2025. The largest single allocation in this act — ₱2.98 billion for the Basic Integration for Harmonized Intervention programme — is the likely source.
A barangay gets a new water supply system. ₱141.0 million was appropriated here for the water supply programme under public works.

A resident wants to know who won the contract for a road in their municipality. Section 13 requires the agency to post the project title, location, description, budget estimates and winning contractor within 30 days of entering the contract.
A ministry stops filing its accountability reports. Section 12 automatically suspends the salaries of the responsible officials until they comply.

key_provisions: Section 1 — Appropriation of Funds. The amounts are appropriated “out of the unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury for the operation of the Bangsamoro Government”. Agency totals for the FY 2024 supplemental appropriation are: Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform ₱3,677,848,135; Public Works ₱1,210,224,400; Health ₱1,000,661,574; the Interior and Local Government ₱956,492,335; Basic, Higher and Technical Education ₱375,787,509; Public Order and Safety ₱271,650,000; Social Services and Development ₱195,002,933; Science and Technology ₱194,578,999; Labor and Employment ₱148,385,580; Transportation and Communications ₱129,248,710; Human Settlements and Development ₱112,800,000; the Bangsamoro Youth Commission ₱69,450,000; Environment, Natural Resources and Energy ₱45,230,500; the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' ₱38,508,800; the Bangsamoro Sports Commission ₱7,500,000; Trade, Investment and Tourism ₱4,500,000; and Indigenous Peoples' Affairs ₱3,392,500 — a total of ₱8,441,261,975.

Section 1 (programme detail) — Among the larger programme lines: Basic Integration for Harmonized Intervention ₱2,983,428,351 and Integrated and Sustainable Development for Aquaculture/Capture ₱633,928,429 under agriculture; Other Infrastructure ₱704,520,600 and Road Network Development ₱294,633,800 under public works; Rapid Emergency Action on Disaster Incidence Services ₱512,315,000 and Interior Affairs Services ₱232,027,900 under the interior ministry; Non-Communicable Disease Cluster ₱298,427,374, Tiyakap Bangsamoro Kalusugan ₱237,375,000, Barangay Health Workers Program ₱124,560,000 and Nutrition Program ₱121,061,300 under health; School-Based Management and Operations ₱173,966,132 and Management Support to Education ₱142,255,577 under education; Peace Building Initiatives ₱168,500,000 and Alternative Dispute Resolution ₱39,000,000 under public order and safety; Employment Facilitation and Promotion ₱148,385,580 under labour; Science Education, Scholarship and Grants ₱93,878,299 under science and technology; and Promulgation of Religious Edicts ₱38,508,800, entirely professional services, under the Darul-Ifta'.

Sections 2–4 (General Provisions) — A Special Allotment Release Order authorises agencies to obligate the appropriations. Government funds are to be used in accordance with the appropriations authorised for the purpose, and agencies must strictly adhere to existing procurement laws, rules and regulations for goods, infrastructure projects and consulting services.

Sections 5–8 — Agencies may deduct engineering and administrative overhead not exceeding 1% of project funds, and administrative costs not exceeding 3% of project costs, for projects costing more than ₱1,000,000. All transportation equipment outlays require the Chief Minister's Authority to Purchase Motor Vehicle on the finance ministry's recommendation, subject to existing guidelines and procurement law. No obligation may be incurred without first securing a Certification of Availability of Funds from the agency's chief accountant, sufficient to cover the contracted activities and made part of the signed contract.

Section 9 — Cash Budgeting System. Appropriations are available for obligation until 31 December 2025, with delivery, inspection and payment valid until funds are fully expended. After the validity period, unreleased appropriations lapse and unobligated funds revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation in accordance with Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054. Funds transferred between organisational units, between agencies, or to local government units are not considered disbursed until the transferred amounts have actually been used to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered, inspected and accepted within the validity period.

Sections 10–12 — Funds are released directly to ministries, offices and agencies, including funds specifically appropriated for their provincial offices and organisational units. Within 60 days of receiving the Commission on Audit's annual audit report, agencies must submit a status report on actions taken on audit findings and recommendations, furnishing copies to the finance ministry, the Speaker and Parliament's Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, and ensuring it is posted on the agency website. Agencies must submit financial and physical accountability reports monthly, quarterly or yearly through the Unified Reporting System, in hardcopy to the finance ministry, and on their websites. “Failure to comply with any of the foregoing shall result in the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until they have complied”, with repeated failure a ground for administrative disciplinary action.

Sections 13–15 — Transparency in Infrastructure Projects requires agencies to post on their websites the project title, location and detailed description, the detailed estimates behind the Approved Budget for the Contract, and the winning contractor with the detailed estimates of the bid as awarded, within 30 calendar days of entering into the contract; and the detailed actual cost of the project with any variation orders, within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion. Ministers, heads of offices and web administrators are responsible for compliance. A separability clause follows, and the act takes effect 15 days after publication in any newspaper of general circulation in the region.

related_legislation.related_note: Supplements the FY 2024 annual appropriations act. Reversion of unobligated funds follows Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054, the Organic Law. The automatic salary suspension for non-reporting in Section 12 anticipates the same mechanism later codified generally in Section 75 of BAA 84, the Bangsamoro Budget System Act of 2025, as does the cash budgeting system in Section 9.

citizen_questions.q: Where did this money come from?
citizen_questions.a: From unutilised prior years' appropriations held in the Bangsamoro Treasury — money that earlier budgets had appropriated but never spent. It is not new revenue.

citizen_questions.q: How much was it in total?

citizen_questions.a: The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, with ₱3,677,848,135 — 43.6% of the whole act. Public works, health and the interior ministry follow, and together those 4 account for about 81% of the total.
The Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, with ₱3,392,500 — about 0.04% of the act, and less than a tenth of the ₱38,508,800 appropriated to the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'.

No. Section 9 made the appropriations available for obligation only until 31 December 2025. Unreleased appropriations lapsed, and unobligated funds reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation.

citizen_questions.q: Can I find out who built a project funded by this act?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Section 13 requires the implementing agency to post on its website the project title, location and description, the estimates behind the approved budget, and the winning contractor with its bid estimates, within 30 days of signing the contract — and the actual cost and any variation orders within 30 days of the completion certificate.

citizen_questions.q: What happens if an agency does not report on its spending?
citizen_questions.a: The salaries of the responsible official or employee are automatically suspended until they comply, and repeated failure without justifiable cause may be a ground for administrative disciplinary action.

views.simple: A ₱8.44 billion supplemental budget for 2024, funded entirely out of appropriations from earlier years that were never spent. Agriculture, fisheries and agrarian reform took ₱3.68 billion, public works ₱1.21 billion, health ₱1.00 billion and the interior ministry ₱956.5 million. Funds were obligable until 31 December 2025, with agencies required to publish infrastructure contracts and costs and facing automatic salary suspension for failing to file accountability reports.
